Built-in Debugger

includes a built-in runtime debugger that captures deterministic execution traces of the Vault pipeline for individual instances. The debugger records pipeline activity, controller decisions, lifecycle transitions, and error events during application execution.

When enabled, the debugger appears as a lightweight floating panel in the browser. From this panel developers can start or stop recording sessions, inspect event counts, export diagnostic logs, and generate AI-assisted debugging reports.

The debugger does not alter pipeline behavior. It operates as a passive observer that records runtime signals emitted by the execution engine.

The debugger reconstructs execution traces by listening to Insight events emitted by instances during Vault pipeline execution. Each recorded event represents a lifecycle transition, controller action, or runtime signal occurring within the pipeline.

By aggregating these events into deterministic traces, the debugger allows engineers to inspect pipeline behavior, analyze performance, and reproduce runtime conditions outside of the running application.

For a deeper explanation of how runtime events are captured and monitored, see Vault Monitor.

Try it in StackBlitz: Built-in Debugger →

TL;DR
↑ top

The fastest way to use the built-in debugger is to enable development mode, record a session, and export the diagnostic logs.

  1. Enable the debugger using devMode: true.
  2. Run your application and open it in a browser.
  3. Click Record in the debugger panel to start capturing pipeline activity.
  4. Trigger the application behavior you want to inspect.
  5. Click Download Logs to export the debug dump.
  6. Optionally use AI Assist to generate an automated diagnostic report.

In most cases the workflow is simple: enable dev mode, record a session, reproduce the issue, download the debug dump, and analyze it with AI Assist.

When to Use the Debugger
↑ top

The built-in debugger is designed to help engineers inspect runtime behavior inside the Vault pipeline. It is particularly useful when investigating complex execution flows or performance issues.

  • Investigating unexpected pipeline behavior.
  • Tracing lifecycle transitions across FeatureCells.
  • Identifying performance bottlenecks in pipeline stages.
  • Debugging controller policy conflicts.
  • Generating diagnostic reports for issue tracking.

Debugger UI

Enabling the Debugger
↑ top

The built-in debugger is available when the Vault runtime is initialized in development mode.

To enable the debugger, configure the Vault runtime with devMode: true. 

{{`// app.config.ts
export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ 
      devMode: true,
    })
  ]
};`}}
 
{{`Vault({
  devMode: true,
});`}}
 
{{`// main.ts
Vault({
  devMode: true,
});`}}

When development mode is active, the debugger widget becomes available and can be attached to the application runtime.

Debug recording captures additional runtime telemetry when a is configured with insights enabled. Insight signals may include error activity, payload information, and committed state snapshots. 

{{`// app.config.ts

export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideVault({ devMode: true }),

    provideFeatureCell(
      EmployeeService,
      {
        key: 'employees',
        initialState: [],
        insights: {
          id: 'employees-insight',
          wantsState: true,
          wantsPayload: true,
          wantsErrors: true
        }
      }
    )
  ]
};`}}
 
{{`export const employeeCell = FeatureCell({
  key: 'employees',
  initialState: [],
  insights: {
    id: 'employees-insight',
    wantsState: true,
    wantsPayload: true,
    wantsErrors: true
  }
});`}}
 
{{`export const employeeCell = FeatureCell({
  key: 'employees',
  initialState: [],
  insights: {
    id: 'employees-insight',
    wantsState: true,
    wantsPayload: true,
    wantsErrors: true
  }
});`}}
Debugger Architecture
↑ top

The debugger operates as a passive observer of the Vault execution engine using the Vault Monitor in debug mode. During pipeline execution, FeatureCells emit insight events describing lifecycle transitions, controller activity, and state updates.

When recording is enabled, these events are captured by the debugger and stored in an in-memory execution trace. The debugger then aggregates this trace into structured diagnostic data that can be exported, analyzed offline, or processed by AI-assisted diagnostic tools.

Because the debugger only listens to emitted signals, it does not alter pipeline execution or affect application behavior.

Typical debug exports are relatively small, often ranging between 50–100 KB when recording standard pipeline activity. However, when wantsState is enabled, the debugger records full FeatureCell state snapshots for each relevant event. Because state objects can be large and may change frequently during execution, exported debug dumps can grow quickly and may reach 10–20 MB depending on application behavior.

This additional detail can be extremely valuable when diagnosing complex issues, but it is recommended to enable state recording only when deeper inspection of application state is required.

Recording Debug Sessions
↑ top

Debug recording sessions capture runtime execution events emitted by the Insight-enabled instances operating within the Vault pipeline. These events include lifecycle transitions, controller activity, pipeline stage execution, and error signals.

Recording sessions begin when the Record button is activated from the debugger panel. Once recording begins, the debugger continuously captures execution signals until recording is stopped.

Recording operates as a passive observer and does not alter pipeline execution behavior. It reacts only to events emitted by the VaultMonitor during pipeline execution.

While recording is active, the debugger displays a session timer and continuously updates the total number of recorded events and detected error events.

Recording can be stopped at any time. When stopped, the captured execution history remains available for export or diagnostic analysis.

Debugger Panel Overview
↑ top

The debugger appears as a movable panel within the browser window. The panel can be repositioned and minimized without interrupting the recording session.

The panel provides the following operational controls:

Debugger Panel Controls
Control Description
Record / Stop Begins or ends a debug recording session. When recording is active, the debugger continuously captures execution events emitted by insight-enabled FeatureCells.
Event Count Displays the total number of execution events captured during the current recording session.
Error Count Displays the number of captured events that include error signals emitted by the pipeline.
Clear Clears all recorded events from the current session and resets the debugger state.
Download Logs Exports the recorded execution trace as a diagnostic dump file that can be inspected or shared for debugging.
AI Assist Generates an AI-assisted diagnostic report using the recorded execution trace.
Create Issue Generates a structured issue report containing the recorded trace data to assist with debugging or filing a repository issue.

The debugger panel state and position are persisted locally in the browser so that the panel appears in the same location across sessions.

Exporting Debug Artifacts
↑ top

The built-in debugger allows engineers to export recorded execution sessions as structured diagnostic artifacts. These exports capture the internal behavior of the Vault pipeline and can be analyzed outside of the running application.

Exported artifacts include structured debug dumps and timeline traces that describe pipeline activity, execution ordering, performance characteristics, and runtime context.

These artifacts are designed for offline inspection, performance analysis, and automated diagnostics. They can be opened in development tools, shared with engineering teams, or attached to issue reports when investigating unexpected pipeline behavior.

Available Export Formats
  • Debug Dump — Structured JSON containing the full recorded event timeline and runtime metadata.
  • Chrome Trace Timeline — Performance trace file that can be opened in Chrome DevTools to visualize pipeline execution as a timeline.
Download Logs (Exporting Diagnostic Logs)
↑ top

Recorded execution sessions can be exported as structured diagnostic logs. These logs contain the complete recorded event timeline captured by the debugger.

Exported logs can be analyzed offline, attached to issue reports, or used for deeper diagnostic analysis of pipeline behavior.

Exporting logs does not clear the current recording session. Developers may export multiple times during a debugging session.

See the Debug Dump Schema for full details.

How To
  • Locate the Download Logs button in the debugger panel.
  • Select the button to export the currently recorded session.
  • The debugger downloads the structured debug dump JSON file.
Chrome Trace Timeline
↑ top

In addition to the structured debug dump, the debugger can export execution traces in Chrome Trace format. This format allows the recorded pipeline activity to be visualized as an interactive flame timeline using Chrome DevTools or other compatible trace viewers.

The exported trace reconstructs pipeline activity using the recorded execution events. Each pipeline stage appears as a timed span in the timeline, allowing engineers to inspect execution ordering, stage durations, and trace fan-out behavior across pipelines.

Trace exports are useful when analyzing pipeline performance, identifying execution bottlenecks, or understanding how multiple traces overlap during runtime.

Trace Export Options

Two trace export modes are available. Both contain the same recorded execution data but differ in how time is represented in the visualization.

  • Actual Time
    Exports the trace using the real measured execution timestamps captured by the debugger. Because pipeline stages typically execute extremely quickly, many spans may appear very short or nearly invisible in timeline viewers.
  • 1000× Zoom
    Exports the same execution trace but expands very small timing gaps to improve visibility in timeline tools. This mode does not change the recorded ordering or behavior of the pipeline—it only scales timing for visualization so that individual stages are easier to inspect.

In most cases the 1000× zoom trace is easier to inspect when analyzing pipeline execution visually, while the actual time trace preserves the precise recorded timings.

Compatible Trace Viewers
  • Chrome DevTools Performance panel
  • Chrome Trace Viewer (chrome://tracing)
  • Perfetto timeline viewer
AI Assist
↑ top

AI Assist exports a diagnostic bundle designed for automated analysis by large language models. The bundle contains the recorded debug dump together with a structured analysis prompt that instructs an AI system how to interpret the captured runtime data.

When supplied to an AI model, the debug dump and prompt enable automated inspection of pipeline execution behavior including stage timings, lifecycle transitions, controller activity, and structural runtime signals. The generated report can help engineers identify performance bottlenecks, investigate pipeline behavior, and perform root-cause analysis of complex runtime issues.

AI Analysis Workflow
  • Click the AI Assist button in the debugger panel.
  • Download the generated SDuX debug JSON file and AI analysis prompt.
  • Upload the debug JSON file directly to the AI model (do not paste the JSON contents).
  • Submit the provided prompt together with the uploaded file.
  • Review and share the generated structured analysis report with your engineering team.

The debugger does not perform the analysis itself. Instead, it prepares a diagnostic bundle that allows external AI systems to evaluate the recorded execution trace and produce a structured engineering report.

AI Assist works with modern large language models capable of analyzing structured JSON files and long diagnostic prompts. The generated analysis prompt is designed to work reliably with the following models.

Supported AI Models
  • OpenAI — GPT-4.1, GPT-4o, GPT-5
  • Anthropic — Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3.7 Sonnet
  • Google — Gemini 1.5 Pro, Gemini 2.0
  • Meta — Llama 3.1 (large context variants)

In most cases the workflow is simple: enable dev mode, record a session, reproduce the issue, download the debug dump, and analyze it with AI Assist.

How To
  • Locate the AI Assist button in the debugger panel.
  • Select the button to download the recorded debug dump and AI analysis prompt.
  • Upload the debug dump JSON file to an AI model.
  • Submit the provided analysis prompt alongside the uploaded file.
  • Review the generated diagnostic report.

AI Assist Reports
↑ top

AI Assist reports are AI-generated diagnostic analyses produced from exported debugger sessions. The report evaluates the recorded execution trace and summarizes runtime behavior across the Vault pipeline.

Using the structured debug dump and analysis prompt, an AI model inspects the captured event timeline, pipeline stage timings, controller activity, and structural runtime signals to produce a detailed engineering report.

The resulting report helps engineers investigate performance bottlenecks, identify pipeline anomalies, and understand execution behavior during complex runtime scenarios.

AI Assist Diagnostic Metrics
↑ top

AI Assist reports include a structured set of diagnostic metrics and visualizations that describe the captured execution session. These diagnostics analyze event distribution, pipeline stage performance, scheduling behavior, state mutation patterns, and structural integrity signals detected during execution.

By aggregating these metrics across traces and pipeline stages, the report highlights performance hotspots, latency sources, recursion risks, and runtime pressure indicators within the Vault pipeline.

AI Assist Diagnostics Overview
Chart / Metric Description How to Use It
Executive Summary High-level diagnostic overview identifying the most significant runtime signal observed during the session. This may include dominant stages, abnormal traces, latency signals, or structural anomalies. Start analysis here. The summary highlights the most important optimization target detected by the diagnostic engine.
Diagnostic Summary Key diagnostic indicators including dominant pipeline stages, longest traces, fan-out signals, and potential deadlock indicators. Quickly determine whether the pipeline is suffering from trace explosion, excessive branching, or stage dominance.
Global Event Metrics Overview of recorded execution activity including total event count, error events, session duration, and overall event timeline. Helps determine overall pipeline activity level and verify whether abnormal event volumes or error bursts occurred during the session.
Timestamp Quantization Analysis Measures timestamp precision and collision rates across recorded events to determine the reliability of timing data. If collision rates are high, stage latency values may be under-resolved. Consider enabling higher-resolution instrumentation.
Event Type Distribution Distribution chart showing how frequently each pipeline event type occurred during the session. Helps verify lifecycle symmetry and detect missing or imbalanced stage transitions in the pipeline.
Stage Latency Aggregates Aggregated timing statistics for each pipeline stage including average duration, P95 latency, and maximum execution time. Identify slow stages and determine which pipeline operations contribute most to compute cost.
Pipeline Flamegraph Visual breakdown of pipeline stage execution time across recorded traces, showing which stages consume the largest share of compute time. Use this view to quickly locate pipeline bottlenecks and high-latency execution stages.
Stage Dominance Analysis Calculates the percentage of total compute time consumed by each stage across the entire session. Detect stages that dominate execution cost and may require optimization.
State Volume Metrics Measures the size and volume of state snapshots emitted during pipeline execution. Helps identify large state payloads or excessive snapshot sizes that may impact performance.
State Churn Analysis Tracks the rate of state mutations and updates per second across the session. Detect excessive update frequency that may indicate redundant pipeline triggers or unnecessary updates.
State Structure Quality Evaluates state complexity including nesting depth, object size, repeated identical states, and structural entropy. Identify redundant state emissions or overly complex state shapes that can be simplified.
Payload Analytics Analyzes payload size and structure for values entering the pipeline. Helps detect oversized payloads or unnecessary data being passed through the pipeline.
Scheduler & Event Loop Analysis Shows how pipeline execution interacts with the JavaScript event loop, including microtask, macrotask, and delayed scheduling. Detect excessive scheduling pressure or event loop contention.
User Interaction Latency Measures delays between pipeline traces to identify gaps caused by user input or application activity. Helps distinguish pipeline latency from user interaction delays.
Burst Analysis Detects bursts of pipeline activity occurring within a single frame or scheduling window. Identify event bursts that may cause frame pressure or UI responsiveness issues.
Trace Analysis Ranks execution traces by duration and event volume to identify unusually long pipeline runs. Use this metric to locate problematic traces that trigger excessive pipeline activity.
Jank & Long Task Correlation Detects long browser tasks that occur alongside pipeline execution. Determine whether UI jank or frame drops correlate with pipeline activity.
Determinism & Structural Integrity Verifies execution determinism by checking for out-of-order events, duplicate traces, or nondeterministic signals. Confirm that pipeline execution remains deterministic and reproducible.
Pipeline Bottleneck Detection Identifies the most likely runtime bottleneck across all diagnostic signals. Focus optimization efforts on the bottleneck stage or behavior identified by the report.
System Health Score Overall diagnostic rating derived from execution stability, performance metrics, and structural signals. Provides a quick indication of overall pipeline health and stability.
Create Issue
↑ top

The debugger can generate a structured issue report containing the captured execution trace from a debugging session.

This report can be attached to GitHub issues when reporting unexpected runtime behavior, controller policy conflicts, or pipeline execution anomalies.

Because the report includes the deterministic event history of the session, maintainers can reproduce and analyze the observed runtime behavior more effectively.

When submitting issue reports, certain diagnostic signals are required to help maintainers reproduce and analyze the reported behavior. Error and payload telemetry provide critical context about pipeline failures and controller activity. State snapshots may optionally be included but should be enabled only when appropriate, as state data can contain sensitive application information.

  • wantsErrors — Required. Ensures error events are included in the diagnostic report.
  • wantsPayload — Required. Captures operation payloads needed to understand event context.
  • wantsState — Optional. Includes FeatureCell state snapshots and may contain sensitive data.
How To
  • Locate the Create Issue button in the debugger panel.
  • Select the button to generate an issue report for the current session.
  • The debugger will prepare a diagnostic dump and redirect you to GitHub.
  • Attach the generated report to the issue submission.
  • Provide a brief description of the observed behavior before submitting.
Debug Dump Overview
↑ top

When a debug session is exported from the built-in debugger, the recorded execution history is written to a structured DebugWidgetDumpShape (diagnostic dump). The dump captures the full runtime context of the session, including pipeline events, environment metadata, performance signals, and aggregated execution statistics.

The export format is deterministic and machine-readable. Each section of the dump represents a specific category of diagnostic data, allowing engineers and automated tools to analyze pipeline behavior, detect anomalies, and reproduce execution conditions outside of the running application.

The tables below document the complete schema of the exported debug dump. They describe the structure of the diagnostic payload, the shape of execution events, captured runtime environment metadata, and the aggregated statistics generated from the recorded event stream.

For automated analysis, use the AI Assist feature. It generates a structured diagnostic report from the exported dump without requiring manual inspection.
